claims.text: The ability of CrFeCoNiX alloys to sustain a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide above 900 °C is controlled by the partitioning behavior of X during oxidation.
Al preferentially diffuses to the oxide/substrate interface during oxidation.
Al partitioning fosters formation of a chemically homogeneous Al2O3 corundum scale.
The Al2O3 scale is thermally matched to the CrFeCoNiX substrate.
Si- or Mn-containing variants form more compositionally heterogeneous oxide scales than Al-containing variants.
Oxides formed when X is Si or Mn have greater thermal-expansion mismatch with the substrate.
Greater thermal-expansion mismatch increases interfacial stress and eventually causes oxide cracking or spallation.
A continuous, compositionally homogeneous oxide scale minimizes thermal-expansion mismatch and interfacial stress accumulation.
Sufficient Al produces a slow-growing, defect-scarce Al2O3 scale.
Close matching of the Al2O3 and substrate thermal-expansion coefficients limits stress buildup.
Higher-Al alloys will develop a continuous, adherent, slow-growing Al2O3 layer with minimal cracking or spallation.
Si- or Mn-rich alloys will exhibit less coherent scales with more cracking, delamination, or spallation after comparable exposure.
Low-Al alloys or alloys lacking effective elemental partitioning will form unstable, rapidly growing oxide scales that fail under thermal cycling.
The proposed mechanism applies to single- or multiphase solid-solution CrFeCoNiX alloys above 900 °C in oxidative or corrosive environments.
